name: Ibn Khaldun
info: Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406) was an Arab scholar, historian and judge, born in Tunis, who served rulers across North Africa and in Granada and wrote the Muqaddimah, an introduction to history regarded as a forerunner of sociology and economics.

facts.born: 26 or 27 May 1332 (1 Ramadan 732 AH) in Tunis, into the Banū Khaldūn, an upper-class Andalusian family of Yemeni Arab descent
facts.died: 17 March 1406, after his last years in Cairo, one month after his sixth selection as Maliki qadi; no cause is given
facts.role: Seal-bearer in the chancellery at Tunis from the age of 20; secretary and minister at the Marinid court in Fez; envoy of Muhammad V of Granada to Castile, 1364; prime minister to the Hafsid sultan of Béjaïa; professor and Grand qadi of the Maliki school in Cairo from 1384, called to the judgeship six times
facts.known: The Muqaddimah; the universal history Kitāb al-ʻIbar; the concept of aṣabiyyah, group solidarity; a theory of the rise and decline of dynasties; early ideas on the division of labour and taxation; his meetings with Timur; his autobiography

t: Ibn Khaldun spent some twenty years in the service of rival North African and Andalusian courts, changing sides often and going to prison for it.
In seclusion at Qalat Ibn Salama he wrote the Muqaddimah, which explains the rise and fall of dynasties through aṣabiyyah, the cohesion of a group.
He passed his last decades in Mamluk Egypt as a teacher and judge; his method had few followers in his time and was taken up by Ottoman and then European scholars centuries later.
dyk: During Timur's siege of Damascus, Ibn Khaldun was lowered over the city wall by ropes to negotiate with the conqueror, who questioned him in detail about the lands of the Maghreb.
ev: Ibn Khaldun is born in Tunis into the Banū Khaldūn, a family that had left Seville a century earlier
After Tunis is defeated by the sultan of Constantine he follows his teacher al-Ābilī to Fez
His scheming against the Marinid sultan Abū Inan earns him a prison sentence of 22 months
Muhammad V of Granada sends him to Pedro the Cruel of Castile to endorse a peace treaty
He returns to Tunis after more than three years at Qalat Ibn Salama, where he wrote the Muqaddimah
The Egyptian sultan Barquq makes him a professor and Grand qadi of the Maliki school in Cairo
He negotiates with Timur outside besieged Damascus
He dies a month after his sixth appointment as Maliki qadi

sections.early:
ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Khaldūn was born in Tunis on 26 May 1332 (1 Ramadan 732 AH) into the Banū Khaldūn, an upper-class Andalusian family of Yemeni Arab descent. He traced his ancestry to Ḥaḍramawt and to Wāʾil Ibn Hujr, a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. The family had been among the leading Arab houses of Seville, where it served as viziers under the Abbadid dynasty; it left the city in 1232, before its occupation in 1248, and settled first in Ceuta and then in Tunis. There his forebears held office under the Hafsid rulers. His great-grandfather, a director of finances, was arrested, tortured and executed during an anti-Hafsid revolt; his grandfather avoided higher appointments and retired to religious scholarship; his father stayed out of politics and devoted himself to fiqh, literature and piety.

His father was his first and most influential teacher. Ibn Khaldun studied Quranic recitation, Maliki law, hadith, poetry and Arabic, became a hafiz at a young age, and received ijazas from the leading hadith scholar in Tunis among others. During the Marinid occupation of Ifriqiya he studied philosophy, logic and mathematics under Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Ābilī, whom he called "the grand master of the rational sciences"; at 19, under al-Ābilī, he completed an abridgement of a work by Fakhr al-Din al-Razi.

The Black Death was a turning point of his youth. It killed his mother and father, much of his extended family and many of his teachers. Douglas H. Garrison and Allen Fromherz argue that the plague shaped his views on urban life and helped inspire the Muqaddimah.
sections.rise:
At the age of 20 Ibn Khaldun began his political career in the chancellery of the Tunisian ruler Ibn Tafrakin as seal-bearer, writing the introductory notes of official documents in fine calligraphy. In 1352 the sultan of Constantine defeated Tunis, and Ibn Khaldun, unhappy with a respected but politically meaningless post, followed al-Ābilī to Fez. The Marinid sultan Abū Inan Fares I appointed him a writer of royal proclamations, but he schemed against his employer and in 1357, aged 25, received a 22-month prison sentence. Freed and reinstated after Abū Inan's death in 1358, he schemed again, this time for the exiled Abū Salem, who on coming to power gave him a ministerial position.

After Abū Salem's fall he received no significant office and moved to Granada, whose Nasrid sultan Muhammad V he had helped at Fez to regain power. In 1364 Muhammad sent him to Pedro the Cruel, king of Castile, to endorse a peace treaty; he declined Pedro's offer to stay at his court and recover his family's Spanish possessions. Rivalry with the vizier Ibn al-Khatib ended in his return to North Africa.

The Hafsid sultan of Béjaïa, Abū ʻAbdallāh, once his companion in prison, made him prime minister, and he carried out a daring mission to collect taxes among the Berber tribes. After the sultan's death in 1366 he changed sides again and allied himself with the sultan of Tlemcen. A few years later he was taken prisoner by Abu Faris Abdul Aziz and withdrew to a religious establishment until 1370; he later resided at Fez under the regent's patronage.
sections.deeds:
Tired of politics and of switching allegiances, Ibn Khaldun took refuge after 1375 with a Berber tribe at Qalat Ibn Salama in the west of Algeria. He lived there over three years and wrote the Muqaddimah, the introduction to his planned history of the world; by his autobiography it took six months. Lacking the texts he needed, he returned in 1378 to Tunis, where he completed the history. The Kitāb al-ʻIbar, the "Book of Lessons", began as a history of the Berbers and grew into a universal history in seven books: the Muqaddimah, a world history to his own time, and a history of the Berbers and the Maghreb that remains an invaluable source.

The Muqaddimah rests on the concept of aṣabiyyah, "group cohesiveness" or "solidarity". This cohesion arises spontaneously in tribes and small kinship groups and can be enlarged by a religious ideology; it carries a group to power but holds the seeds of its downfall, when a new group bound by a stronger cohesion replaces it. A society moves from nomadic to sedentary life and to refinement in crafts and arts, then weakens and is conquered, and the cycle repeats.

He called for a science to explain society. He rejected Muslim historians' focus on the credibility of a report's transmitter in favour of testing the validity of the stories themselves. He held the state necessary to restrain injustice, though its means, force, is itself an injustice. He outlined early theories of the division of labour, taxes, scarcity and economic growth; Ibrahim Oweiss argues that he originated the labor theory of value long before Adam Smith and David Ricardo.
sections.opponents:
Ibn Khaldun made enemies at every court he served. In Granada the vizier Ibn al-Khatib viewed his closeness to Muhammad V with mistrust and thought his attempt to shape the young sultan into an ideal ruler foolish and a danger to peace; through his influence Ibn Khaldun was sent back to North Africa. In Tunis the ruler Abū l-Abbas questioned his loyalty, the more so when Ibn Khaldun presented him with a copy of his history that omitted the usual panegyric to the ruler. His own career of plots and changed allegiances had twice put him in prison.

In Egypt his efforts to reform what he believed to be abuses in the administration of justice met resistance, and within a year he had to resign his judgeship. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, a contemporary, accused him of inadequate historical knowledge, an inaccurate title and disorganisation, and noted that he was not well liked in Egypt because he opposed respected traditions, including the traditional judicial dress. He fell from favour at the Mamluk court for joining, apparently under duress, a fatwa against Sultan Barquq, and in old age was arrested over an alleged link to a reform-minded underground party.

Later readers have found faults of their own. Some of his views, particularly on the Zanj people of sub-Saharan Africa, have been cited as racist. He synthesised sources without citations and reproduced some errors from a 14th-century Fez source. Reynold A. Nicholson praised him but discounted his influence, and some scholars judge the praise of his student al-Maqrizi empty and lacking understanding of his methods.
sections.last:
Ibn Khaldun left Tunis under the pretence of going on the Hajj, for which a Muslim ruler could not refuse permission, and sailed to Alexandria. Of Egypt he said, "He who has not seen it does not know the power of Islam." In 1384 the Mamluk sultan Barquq made him professor of the Qamhiyyah Madrasah and Grand qadi of the Maliki school of law. In the same year a ship carrying his wife and children sank off Alexandria. After returning from a pilgrimage to Mecca in May 1388 he concentrated on teaching in Cairo madrasas. Relations with Barquq recovered after the affair of the fatwa and he was again named Maliki qadi; altogether he was called six times to that office, which he never held long.

In 1401, under Barquq's son Faraj, he took part, against his own doubts, in a campaign against Timur, who had besieged Damascus in 1400. Faraj, worried by a revolt in Egypt, hurried home and left his army in Syria. Ibn Khaldun remained at the besieged city for seven weeks and was lowered over the wall by ropes to negotiate with Timur, in a series of meetings he reported extensively in his autobiography. Timur questioned him about the Maghreb, and at his request Ibn Khaldun wrote a long report on it. Back in Egypt he composed a report on the history of the Tatars and a character study of Timur for the Marinid rulers in Fez.

He spent the next five years in Cairo completing his autobiography and his history and acting as teacher and judge. He died on 17 March 1406, one month after his sixth selection as Maliki qadi.
sections.legacy:
Ibn Khaldun's historical method had very few precedents or followers in his own time, and only a few of his students knew the Muqaddimah. An exception was the jurist Ibn al-Azraq, who quoted heavily from his history. Ottoman intellectuals took him up in the 17th century: Kâtip Çelebi named him as a great influence, and Mustafa Naima used his cyclical theory to describe the Ottoman Empire.

In Europe a biography of him appeared in 1697 in Barthélemy d'Herbelot's Bibliothèque Orientale. From 1806 Silvestre de Sacy published his biography with translated parts of the Muqaddimah, and the complete Arabic edition appeared in 1858. Robert Flint wrote that "as a theorist of history he had no equal in any age or country until Vico appeared"; Arnold J. Toynbee called the Muqaddimah "the greatest work of its kind"; Ernest Gellner considered his definition of government the best in the history of political theory. His ideas have been compared with those of Machiavelli, Vico, Hegel, Marx, Comte, Ricardo and Adam Smith, as precedents and not direct influences. More moderate views of his contributions have also emerged, and Abdelmajid Hannoum holds that the translator de Slane wrongly read a racial opposition of Arabs and Berbers into the history.

Economists have claimed him too. Paul Krugman described him as the philosopher "who basically invented what we would now call the social sciences", Arthur Laffer acknowledged that his ideas precede the Laffer curve, and in 1981 Ronald Reagan cited him on taxation. In 2006 Spain marked the 600th anniversary of his death with an exhibition.

summary: Born in Tunis to an Andalusian family, Ibn Khaldun served and plotted at the courts of North Africa and Granada before writing the Muqaddimah, which explains the rise and decline of dynasties through group solidarity. He ended his life as a teacher and judge in Mamluk Cairo.

notes: Birth date: the article's lead gives 27 May 1332, its Birth and family section 26 May 1332 (1 Ramadan 732 AH). I used 26 May and flagged the other in the facts.
Place of death: the article does not state it outright; it says he spent his last five years in Cairo and then gives the date. I wrote 'after his last years in Cairo'.

Arrival in Egypt: the article gives no year for the sailing to Alexandria; al-Sakhāwī is cited for arrival in Cairo in Shaʿbān 782 AH/1380 CE, while the title of Fischel's book has 1382-1406. I gave no year.
The Black Death has no date in the article; none given.
The article says he 'entered a monastic establishment' until 1370; I wrote 'withdrew to a religious establishment'. The editor may prefer the article's words.

The article's passage on Abū Salem is garbled ('schemed against Abū Inan's successor, Abū Salem Ibrahim III, with Abū Salem's exiled uncle, Abū Salem'); I wrote only that he schemed for the exiled Abū Salem, who gave him a ministerial post.
